steps.body: The habit that separates pros: **every exact answer gets a one-glance guard**. Before trusting 512 − 289 = 223, think 500 − 300 = 200 — the answer sits nearby, so it survives. You built this guard in the rounding chapter; now it goes on permanent duty.
Post the guard before the exact work.

widget.prompt: You're about to compute 487 + 316 exactly. First, slide to the guard's estimate.
widget.lowFeedback: Too small — 487 alone is nearly 500. The guard should stand near the friendly sum.
widget.highFeedback: Way past the pile — five hundred plus three hundred can't reach the thousands. Ease back.
widget.successFeedback: Guard posted at ≈800 (500 + 300). The exact answer, 803, reports in right beside it.

predict.prompt: Before computing 487 + 316 exactly: the guard's estimate is about…
predict.reveal: 487 rounds up to 500 and 316 down to 300: about 800. Now the exact answer (803) has a bodyguard — if your computation lands far from 800, the estimate catches the slip before anyone else does.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents estimate check.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for estimate check must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines estimate check.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

steps.body: Some answers are busted before any rounding.
explanationVariants: Taking away can't grow a pile: 762 is bigger than the 623 Ben started with — impossible, no rounding needed.
The size rules from the multiplication course still patrol here: a difference must be smaller than the number you subtract from.

widget.prompt: Ben computes 623 − 385 and writes 762. How do you bust it in ONE glance?

options.label: 762 is bigger than 623 — taking away can't grow the pile
options.feedback: The oldest size rule there is: a subtraction's answer can't beat its starting number. Busted with zero arithmetic.

options.label: You can't know without redoing the subtraction
options.feedback: You can — one glance shows 762 towering over the 623 he started from. Size checks are free.

options.label: 623 must have been copied wrong
options.feedback: Blaming the copy skips the check! Whatever the numbers, an answer LARGER than the start is impossible for subtraction.

options.label: Because 762 ends in 2
options.feedback: The last digit is innocent — plenty of good answers end in 2. It's 762's SIZE that betrays it.

steps.body: The figure shows 349 rounding to 300 because it lies just below the halfway point, 350. Use that same guard routine in three beats: **round the players → one friendly computation → compare**. If an exact answer has the wrong size, redo the computation.
Post the guard for an addition.
explanationVariants: 298 → 300 (tens digit 9) and 447 → 400 (tens digit 4); the guard stands at 300 + 400 = 700.
The exact 745 reports in — within a stone's throw of the 700 guard, so it passes.

widget.prompt: You're checking 298 + 447. What estimate does the guard use? (Round each to the nearest hundred first.)

commonErrors.feedback: 745 is the EXACT sum — the guard wants the friendly version: 300 + 400.
600 rounded 298 DOWN to 200 — but its tens digit is 9, practically banging on 300's door.
800 rounded 447 UP to 500 — but its tens digit is 4, below the middle. 447 stays at 400.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Round both (298 → ?, 447 → ?), then add the friendly hundreds.

widget.prompt: Four answers are offered for 512 − 189. Sort them: pass the ≈300 guard, or busted?

items.feedback: 323 stands right beside the 300 guard — and it happens to be the exact answer.
703 is more than double the guard — it's near the SUM of the two numbers. The operation flipped somewhere. Busted.
123 sits a whole 200 below the guard — a couple of hundreds went missing. Busted.
313 passes the SIZE check even though the exact answer is 323 — guards catch big blunders and honestly miss small slips.

widget.missFeedback: Compare each to 300: within a few dozen passes; hundreds away is busted.
widget.successFeedback: 323 and 313 pass; 703 and 123 are busted. The guard sees size, not digits — powerful, and honest about its limits.

steps.body: The certainty trick returns — round AGAINST yourself.
explanationVariants: Round every class UP (100 + 110 + 130 = 340): if even the inflated classes fit under 350, the real ones must.
Safe-direction rounding stacks the odds against you on purpose — passing anyway makes the yes certain.

widget.prompt: A hall seats 350. Classes of 98, 104, and 121 want in. Using estimates ALONE, can you be sure they all fit?

options.label: Yes — round every class UP (100 + 110 + 130 = 340), and they still fit
options.feedback: The inflated versions total 340 ≤ 350 — and real classes are smaller than their inflations. Certain, with zero exact adding.

options.label: No — three classes never fit in one hall
options.feedback: Check the sizes, not the count: even rounded UP, the three classes total 340 — under the 350 seats.

options.label: Only exact addition can give certainty
options.feedback: Usually — but rounding AGAINST yourself creates certainty too: if the unfair version passes, the fair one must.

options.label: Yes, because halls are usually big
options.feedback: Hall trivia isn't proof! The certainty comes from 340 ≤ 350 with every class deliberately over-counted.

steps.body: Catch the slip, then fix it — the full pro workflow.
hints: Post the guard first: 534 − 267 ≈ 500 − 300 = 200. Nia's 333 stands 133 away — busted.
Her slip: smaller-from-larger in every spot (7−4, 6−3, 5−2 all flipped). Redo with trades.
534 repackages as 4 hundreds, 12 tens, 14 ones — now every spot can pay.
explanationVariants: Nia flipped every short spot. Trading instead: two breaks give 4h 12t 14o, and the honest answer is 267.

widget.prompt: Nia computes 534 − 267 and writes 333. Post the guard, catch her slip, and enter the CORRECT difference.

commonErrors.feedback: 333 is Nia's slip — smaller-from-larger in every spot (7−4, 6−3, 5−2). The guard's 200 busts it: it's 133 too big. Short spots trade down instead.
367 traded for the ones but the tens' own trade never charged the hundreds — after lending, the hundreds hold 4, giving 4 − 2 = 2 up front.
277 is close — off by one ten. After the ones borrowed, the tens hold 12; check 12 − 6 = 6, not 7.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Guard says ≈200. Repackage 534 (4 hundreds, 12 tens, 14 ones), then subtract spot by spot.

steps.body: The guard never goes off duty again.
takeaways: Every exact answer gets a guard: round, compute friendly, compare.
Impossible sizes (a difference bigger than its start) need no rounding at all.
Safe-direction rounding turns estimates into certainty for yes/no questions.
steps.teaser: next chapter: multiplying by tens — where 4 × 60 is just 4 × 6 tens wearing a costume.

concept.body: Quick rewind. The guard is three beats: **round each player, do the friendly version, compare**. Checking 61 − 29? Guard: 60 − 30 = 30. An exact answer near 30 passes; one like 92 is busted on sight.

explanationVariants: 41 → 40 and 38 → 40; the guard stands at 40 + 40 = 80 (the exact 79 is right beside it).
Both players round to 40 — the friendly version is a double.

options.feedback: Both players round to 40; the guard stands at 80, one step from the exact 79.

options.label: 41 + 38 = 79, computed exactly
options.feedback: 79 is the exact work — the guard is the FRIENDLY version posted beside it: 40 + 40.
Both players rounded UP past their closer tens — 41 and 38 each live nearest to 40.
